new.title: The fate of Mercury's ejected mantle
new.summary: Mercury's unusually high core mass fraction, inferred from its high bulk density, remains difficult to explain. Mantle stripping by a giant impact provides a plausible origin, but without efficient removal, the ejected debris remains on Mercury-crossing orbits and later gets re-accreted. Here, we show that re-accretion of impact debris onto Mercury is inefficient, making a giant-impact origin plausible. We combine N-body simulations of giant-impact ejecta with a collisional evolution model and consideration of processes acting on small dust. We find that, when the ejecta are dominated by large, several hundred km-sized non-vaporized fragments, the debris disk remains optically thin and the collisional cascade is truncated near the radiation-pressure blowout limit, where micron-sized grains are removed. In contrast, if vaporized, the ejecta recondense into mm to cm-sized droplets and form an optically thick disk, in which radiation pressure cannot efficiently truncate the cascade. The debris can then be ground down to nanometre-sized grains, where collisions become predominantly non-fragmenting and dissipative rather than destructive. Subsequent inelastic collisions damp the eccentricities and inclinations of the nanodust, producing a geometrically thin disk whose lifetime is governed by removal through exposed surface layers, where grains acquire large charge-to-mass ratios through solar UV radiation and are rapidly removed by electromagnetic forces. In either scenario, collisional evolution strongly reduces the re-accretion of debris and alleviates a key difficulty for the giant-impact origin of Mercury's large core. More broadly, highly energetic giant impacts in the inner regions of planetary systems may lead to short-lived populations of nanometre-sized dust.

new.title: Planetary biotechnospheres, biotechnosignatures and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence
new.summary: The concept of planetary intelligence as collective intelligence is used to consider possible evolutionary paths of biotechnospheres that emerge on the intersection of the technosphere with the biosphere and support coupling of the technosphere with the biosphere, thus affecting planetary evolution. In mature biotechnospheres, the intelligence of technologies and the intelligence of life forms, including engineered life forms, could act in concert to perform various tasks (e.g. monitoring and restoring planetary environments and biodiversity; supporting space missions; terraforming cosmic objects). Space exploration can expand biotechnospheres beyond planets and create cosmic ecosystems. Humankind, other civilizations or their intelligent machines may produce biotechnosignatures (i.e. observables and artefacts of biotechnospheres) in the Solar System and beyond. I propose ten possible biotechnosignatures and strategies for the search for these biotechnosignatures in situ and over interstellar distances. For example, if a non-human advanced civilization existed and built biotechnospheres on Earth in the past, the descendants of its engineered bacteria could currently exist on Earth and have properties pertaining to the functions of the ancient bacteria in the biotechnospheres; intelligent technologies created by the ancient civilization could migrate to the Solar System's outer regions; these two scenarios are described as the Cosmic Descendants hypothesis. Interstellar asteroids, free-floating planets, spacecraft and objects gravitationally bound to flyby stars might carry extraterrestrial biotechnospheres and pass through the Solar System. In connection to the fate of post-main-sequence stars and their Oort clouds, the probability for interstellar asteroids to carry biotechnospheres or to be interstellar spacecraft is estimated as very low.

new.title: Weak buoyancy and cold lithospheres decouple interior melting from seafloor volcanism on icy ocean worlds
new.summary: On icy ocean worlds, deep silicate melting can generate sufficient pressure to open fractures while magma freezes before reaching the ocean. We identify a coupled transport regime by linking finite melt segregation and nonlinear rock relaxation to fracture flow, crystallisation and the ice-loaded ocean boundary. In a hot Europa endmember, increasing grain size from 1 to 10 mm raises relaxed excess pressure from 5.55 kPa to 10.2 MPa, overcoming the inherited-fracture opening threshold despite weak buoyancy. For the same 100 m strike and 0.5 m aperture, the cold first-fill rate required by heat balance increases from 0.17-0.69 m3 s -1 over terrestrial crustal distances of 1.1-4.5 km to 15-29 m3 s -1 across 89-171 km Europa paths, far above the self-supplied flow. Higher ice-ocean pressure further reduces the enthalpy margin of near-solidus magma in the adopted basalt phase law. During approximately 5 kyr of dormancy, the collector pressure returns to its relaxed value, while upper-path walls cool to 275-282 K and the magma path loses liquid connectivity. In two focused Europa histories with mechanically supported pathways, delivery of 0.005 km3 of magma over 0.1 Myr requires 14-27 km3 of sacrificed magma-equivalent preparation material. Weak gravity, extensive cold rock and a pressurised ocean thus make seafloor access a history-dependent process governed by thermal connectivity and its renewal, decoupling recurrent volcanism from melt production at depth.

new.title: Stellar Obliquities of Cold Jupiter and Brown Dwarf Systems I: Spin-Orbit Misalignment Grows with Orbital Eccentricity
new.summary: Stellar obliquity provides insights into the formation and dynamical evolution of planetary systems. Most obliquity measurements to date have focused on close-in transiting giant planets, whose orbits may have been altered by migration and tidal interactions. In contrast, the stellar obliquities of cold Jupiters, the most common class of giant planets, remain largely unexplored. Here, we measure the minimum stellar obliquity for 69 cold Jupiters and brown dwarfs (M_p > 0.3 M_J, a > 1 au), by comparing stellar inclinations derived from stellar rotation measurements with companion orbital inclinations constrained by radial velocities, relative astrometry and Hipparcos-Gaia absolute astrometry. We find that spin-orbit misalignments are common among cold Jupiters and brown dwarf companions, with 19/69 (28 +6/-5%) exhibiting significant misalignments. Furthermore, the stellar obliquities depends strongly on orbital eccentricity, whereby 0/17 (0 +8/-0%) companions with e_orb <= 0.15 are misaligned, compared to 19/52 (37 +7/-6%) with more eccentric orbits. This pattern reveals a connection between orbital eccentricity and stellar obliquity: companions on nearly circular orbits tend to be aligned with their host stars, whereas those on eccentric orbits exhibit a broader range of obliquities. This finding suggests that post-formation dynamical interactions, such as planet-planet scattering or secular chaos, may play an important role in exciting both orbital eccentricities and spin-orbit misalignments.

new.title: Planetary Habitable Zones around Magnetized White Dwarfs
new.summary: White dwarfs are known to host remnant planetary material, indicating that rocky objects can survive post-main-sequence evolution and migrate into very close orbits. However, the decline of white dwarf luminosity makes it difficult for a planet to remain habitable for long when relying only on the white dwarf's irradiative heating. While several non-radiative energy sources have been proposed, the role of white dwarf magnetism in planetary energy budgets remains largely unexplored. We examine whether magnetic unipolar induction could provide sustained heating for close-in rocky planets. By coupling white dwarf cooling tracks with an orbit-dependent induction model, we evaluate the contribution of ohmic dissipation to planetary surface energy budgets and estimate the upper limit with efficient heat deposition. It is possible for the induction heating to supply a nearly steady surface energy flux for certain orbital distances and stellar spins, partially offsetting the decline in the white dwarf irradiation at late times. This leads to a persistent outer temperate region and, in some cases, a narrow inner zone that emerges after substantial cooling, identifying magnetic induction as a viable long-lived supplement to radiative heating.

new.title: Mass Spectral Evidence for Iron Sulfate in Venus' Cloud Aerosol
new.summary: Venus' cloud aerosols play pivotal roles in the thermal, chemical, and optical properties of the atmosphere. Here, we present mass spectral evidence that the cloud aerosols contain abundant iron sulfates. Data from the Pioneer Venus Large Probe Neutral Mass Spectrometer (LNMS) suggest that cloud aerosols inadvertently collected into the inlets at ~48-51 km and thermally decomposed below the clouds, releasing several compounds into the LNMS. At 23 km and below, multiple iron species (54Fe+, 56FeO+, 54FeO+, 56Fe2O+, and 56Fe2O2+) and other decomposition gases were detected. Quantitative treatment of these mass signals suggested the release of Fe2O3, SO2, O2, SO3, H2SO4, and H2O, consistent with the thermal decomposition of hydronium-bearing ferric sulfates. The resulting mole ratio for iron to sulfate (2.0 +/- 1.1) aligns with hydronium jarosite ((H3O)Fe3(SO4)2(OH)6), which likely formed within the inlets after aerosol capture, dehydration, and loss of sulfuric acid. Our thermochemical calculations support these assessments. Speciation of the ferric sulfates in the native aerosols remains unconstrained (e.g., solution and/or particle phases). Peak fits to the thermal release profiles yielded the abundances of the bulk iron (0.8 +/- 0.4 mg m-3) and aerosol-derived compounds, including hydronium jarosite (2.2 +/- 1.2 mg m-3, 30 +/- 17 wt%), water (3.7 +/- 0.4 mg m-3, 50 +/- 10 wt%), and sulfuric acid (1.5 +/- 0.2 mg m-3, 20 +/- 5 wt%). Surface sourcing of the cloud iron is likely minor. Instead, cosmic dust influx could deliver iron to the clouds in a geologically short time (2.4 +/- 1.5 Myr).

new.title: Discovery of Trailing Spiral Dust Alignment in the Dust Polarization of HL Tau at $λ= 2.1$ mm
new.summary: Polarimetric observations of protoplanetary disks at (sub)millimeter wavelengths constrain dust grain properties, dynamics, and alignment mechanisms. We present new high-resolution ALMA Band 4 (2.1 mm) polarization observations of HL Tau with spatial resolutions of $\sim$0.08$''$ (11.78 au) and $\sim$0.19$''$ (27.99 au). Linearly decomposing the polarization into contributions from dust scattering and thermal emission by aligned grains, we analyze the new Band 4 data and published high-resolution Band 7 (870 $\mu$m) observations. Thermal emission from aligned grains dominates the polarization across the disk at Band 4, in contrast to the scattering-dominated Band 7, and both mechanisms vary radially with the disk substructures, consistent with expected optical depth variations. At Band 4, we detect a coherent angular deviation from purely azimuthal grain alignment, in which the streamlines of the alignment field yield trailing spirals with respect to disk rotation. A single global offset angle quantifies this deviation as $2.83^\circ\pm0.33^\circ$ and $4.10^\circ\pm0.09^\circ$ (statistical uncertainties) from two robust weightings, and the detection reaches a significance of $\approx7\sigma$ under conservative uncertainty estimates. This trailing orientation is consistent with aerodynamic ("badminton birdie-like") alignment driven by gas-dust drift near pressure bumps. However, under an axisymmetric disk velocity structure, this interpretation requires Stokes numbers two to three orders of magnitude larger than expected for the grains dominating the millimeter emission. At Band 7, the polarization angle is weakly sensitive to the alignment direction and exhibits a near/far-side antisymmetric structure that the model cannot reproduce. The Band 7 data therefore neither support nor contradict the Band 4 result.

new.title: A Large Envelope Can Explain Super-Puffs
new.summary: Super-puffs are a class of exoplanets with extremely low bulk densities, having masses of a few to tens of Earth masses but radii comparable to that of Jupiter. Observations suggest that these inflated radii can persist for Gyr timescales, even for planets receiving relatively low stellar irradiation. The physical mechanisms responsible for maintaining such large radii, however, remain poorly understood. Here, we model the thermal evolution of super-puffs with substantial H/He envelopes using a one-dimensional planetary structure and cooling model. We follow the coupled cooling and contraction of the planetary interior and H/He envelope while self-consistently calculating the planet's hydrostatic and radiative--convective structure. We find that planets with H/He envelope mass fractions of approximately $40-60\%$ can retain Jupiter-like radii over Gyr timescales, provided that they begin with sufficiently hot interiors. Massive H/He envelopes substantially delay planetary contraction through two effects: (1) strong thermal blanketing, which slows the cooling of the underlying rocky core, and (2) Kelvin--Helmholtz luminosity generated by the cooling and contraction of the envelope itself, which helps maintain its high entropy and inflated radius. Our results suggest that super-puffs may represent a distinct class of planets that accreted large quantities of nebular gas during formation without undergoing runaway gas accretion.

new.title: The oxygen cold trap in protoplanetary discs
new.summary: The diffusive transport of oxygen in protoplanetary discs followed by sequestration into ice in the midplane, a process known as the cold trap, can substantially alter the chemical environment where planets form. This paper presents a new time-dependent modelling framework that allows us to consistently simulate kinetic gas-phase chemistry, ice growth and desorption, turbulent diffusive mixing, and gravitational settling of icy particles with a changing particle size distribution over million-year timescales in one-dimensional vertical columns. Applying our model to a T Tauri disc across radii from 1 to 100 au reveals that vertical cold trapping becomes an effective mechanism once the diffusion-to-settling timescale ratio exceeds unity, simultaneously driving the gas-phase C/O up toward unity, and the gas-phase C/H down, by up to two orders of magnitude at large distances. All models feature the development of an upward counter-flux due to the turbulent up-whirling of icy particles followed by ice sublimation above the horizontal icelines, which brings the cold trapping to a halt and eventually establishes a relaxed vertical structure after about $10^4$ to $10^6$ yr, depending on the radial distance. The ice formation leads to a strongly peaked size distribution around 1 mic, which contains the majority of the condensed mass in the disc after ice formation, and changes the dynamical behaviour of the grains substantially. We conclude that the vertical cold trap can provide an important part of the explanation why evolved discs observed with ALMA often show high C/O ratios as inferred from strong emissions from hydrocarbon molecules in the outer disc, such as C2H and c-C3H2. However, in none of our models does the C/O ratio exceed unity, which is a consequence of CO-blocking, a chemical process where water molecules naturally stop forming once C/O approaches unity.

cross.title: Halley's Comet Over New Zealand In 1910: An Overview Of A Spectacular Apparition
cross.summary: Halley's Comet (1P/Halley) returns to the inner Solar System approximately every 76 years. In 1910, the comet put on a particularly wonderful display, whereby the comet attained an apparent magnitude of 1 or brighter, and had a tail of up to 120° in length. Many New Zealanders saw Comet 1P/Halley and submitted articles to newspapers across the land. Those articles were mostly from lay-people who reported their observations of this, the most famous of all comets. There were, however, numerous serious amateur and professional astronomers who made detailed observations and took world-class photographs of the comet. In this paper, we present the results of a thorough search through historical records and media publications in Aotearoa/New Zealand, to investigate how extensively Comet 1P/Halley was observed from this island nation. Where appropriate, we compare the observations described with international accounts, and find that those made from Aotearoa/New Zealand often echo what observers were witnessing around the world. We find that thousands of New Zealanders observed Comet 1P/Halley in 1910, and that the comet raised the interest in astronomy across the land resulting in the establishment of a number of astronomical societies that remain active to the current day.

cross.title: OSIRIS-REx Lessons Learned Report: Insights from the Journey to Bennu and Back
cross.summary: OSIRIS-REx, NASA's third New Frontiers mission, was the first U.S. mission to return a sample from an asteroid. Proposed in 2010 for an \$811 million lifecycle cost, the mission was completed for \$828 million, returned more than \$52 million of Headquarters reserves unused, and delivered at least 121.6 g of pristine material from near-Earth asteroid (101955) Bennu in September 2023, more than twice the Level-1 requirement. It did so despite a surface far more rugged than predicted, the discovery of particle ejection, sampling in a regolith much weaker than expected, operations during the COVID-19 pandemic, and an off-nominal parachute sequence on Earth return. This report sets out the lessons learned by the mission's leadership across six areas: leadership and governance; cost, schedule and risk management; systems engineering; mission operations; sample return, curation and analysis; and data archiving. Recurring themes are that a PI-led structure integrating science, engineering and project management gives the discipline to make fast, informed decisions; that reserves and schedule margin spent early to retire risk, such as funding Natural Feature Tracking as a backup navigation system, buy the flexibility to absorb discovery; that heritage hardware reduces risk only when its verification and engineering knowledge are preserved; and that contamination knowledge, sample science and data stewardship are mission-long responsibilities, not post-flight tasks. Each section pairs background with specific recommendations for future sample-return and small-body missions.

cross.title: line racer: Rapid Calculation of Exoplanetary Radiative Opacities
cross.summary: Detailed studies of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres rely on precise knowledge of the spectral features of possible atmospheric species. These features are a result of the interaction of different molecules and atoms with the radiation of the host star or the intrinsic thermal radiation of the object. The interaction is described by the opacity of a species, which determines how much light is absorbed at a given wavelength. The strength and shape of these opacities are very dependent on the temperature and pressure of the atmosphere, which is why they have to be calculated for a wide range of conditions. line racer is a Python package that enables computing high-resolution opacities from large molecular and atomic line lists in an effective manner. It offers users a wide range of options to customize opacity calculations to their needs and available hardware. The code is designed for efficient parallelization on multi-core and multi-node systems and can produce outputs compatible with popular atmospheric modeling and retrieval tools.

cross.title: Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE): A Mission Concept for a Low-Frequency Radio Interferometer on the Lunar Farside
cross.summary: The universe below 20 MHz remains one of space science's last unexplored frontiers, inaccessible from Earth due to its ionosphere and terrestrial radio frequency interference (RFI). We present the mission concept for the Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE), an all-sky imaging, low-frequency radio telescope operating from 100 kHz-30 MHz from the lunar farside, the quietest radio environment in the inner Solar System. If realized, MoonRISE would be the first radio interferometer on the Moon and the first connected-element radio interferometer in space. Its science objectives are to (1) determine how solar wind turbulence drives plasma heating, acceleration, and space weather evolution in the inner heliosphere, by measuring the scattering of type III solar radio bursts between 2-20 solar radii; (2) constrain the density, structure, and variability of the lunar ionosphere and its effects on surface communication; and (3) resolve the plasma sources and magnetospheric dynamics that power Uranian Kilometric Radiation, observable for the first time since Voyager 2 in 1986. The same observations would yield all-sky maps of the low-frequency sky, subsurface structure at the landing site, and a characterization of the farside RF environment. The Radio Interferometer concept consists of nine 3.5 m dipoles embedded in a 1.5 km optical-fiber tether deployed by a rover, with power- and RF-over-fiber enabling RFI-free mapping. A rover-mounted Ground Penetrating Radar (300-2000 MHz) would measure regolith dielectric properties and bedrock depth to characterize the dipoles' RF performance. We describe the science objectives, a reference landing site in Lacus Luxuriae, a notional concept of operations, and the payload design and technology maturity. The concept builds on SunRISE and OVRO-LWA heritage and could serve as a basis for a future selected mission.

cross.title: Formation of Electron Velocity Distribution Functions at low-\{beta} Quasi-Perpendicular Shocks From Physical-Mass-Ratio PIC Simulations
cross.summary: At low-\{beta} quasi-perpendicular shocks, the origins of upstream field-aligned electron beams and downstream flat-top distributions remain unresolved. Using 2D fully kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations at the physical ion-to-electron mass ratio (mi/me = 1836), we found that the shock transition region is dominated by electromagnetic whistler-mode turbulence driven by the modified two-stream instability (MTSI) of reflected ions, not by the electrostatic instabilities as suggested by some previous studies using a reduced mass ratio. Beams in the upstream are produced mainly by shock-drift acceleration (SDA) at the ramp, whereas we attribute the downstream flat-top distributions to nonuniform acceleration by the parallel electric field. Electrons experience different field strengths, polarities, and interaction durations along their trajectories, leading to a spread of parallel velocity changes that broadens and flattens the distribution. These results highlight the importance of using the physical mass ratio in exploring the electron dynamics of low-\{beta} shocks.

cross.title: Graph Parameterization for Invariant Manifolds Attached to Quasi-Periodic Tori
cross.summary: We develop a high-order Fourier-Taylor graph-parameterization method for computing local invariant manifolds attached to reducible quasi-periodic invariant tori of discrete dynamical systems, with particular emphasis on Poincaré maps. Assuming that the invariant torus and its Floquet reduction are known, we represent the manifold as a graph over a selected spectral subspace and compute its coefficients recursively through jet transport and cohomological equations on the torus. The formulation accommodates stable, unstable, and center spectral selections. For center manifolds, it simultaneously determines the nonlinear reduced dynamics, providing a low-dimensional representation from which nearby invariant objects can be lifted to the original phase space. For real systems with complex-conjugate Floquet multipliers, we derive an equivalent real formulation based on Hermitian symmetry and Krawtchouk transformations. This allows real-valued jet transport while retaining the advantages of complex spectral coordinates in the cohomological solver. The implementation also incorporates inverse dynamics for stable directions, multiple shooting, coordinate scaling, and a posteriori validation tests. Numerical experiments with a quasi-periodically forced pendulum, an oscillating solar sail in the Earth-Moon system, and a simplified solar system model illustrate the construction and its computational properties. In the solar-sail benchmark, the real formulation reduces computation time by approximately a factor of 2.2 compared with the complex implementation.

cross.title: NASA's Pandora SmallSat Mission: Gaussian Processes for Simulated Stellar Heterogeneity Corrections under Imperfect Stellar Models
cross.summary: Stellar contamination is the primary bottleneck limiting robust atmospheric characterization of exoplanets orbiting active K- and M-dwarfs with James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) transmission spectroscopy. Launched in January 2026, NASA's Pandora SmallSat mission addresses this challenge through long-term, simultaneous visible photometry and near-infrared spectroscopy of planet-hosting stars, providing the data to disentangle planetary and stellar signals. However, conventional stellar-contamination corrections rely on stellar atmosphere models, making them vulnerable to model inaccuracies that can impede accurate inferences. Here, we investigate how Pandora data can be used to mitigate stellar contamination without an accurate host star model. We present a Gaussian-process-aided stellar retrieval framework that learns wavelength-dependent deviations from current stellar model grids. We propagate stellar contamination factors directly from the stellar retrieval into the planetary atmospheric retrievals, allowing the atmospheric inference to marginalize over stellar-contamination uncertainty without relying on a biased stellar model. Tests using simulated Pandora observations with realistic stellar model mismatch show that this framework consistently improves the recovery of disk-integrated stellar spectra. For a WASP-69 b-like system, this approach can reduce model-driven biases in inferred atmospheric properties, though degeneracies among stellar and atmospheric parameters can leave residual biases. This flexible, data-driven framework is a promising approach toward accurate stellar-contamination corrections and more robust atmospheric inference even when host-star model grids are inaccurate.

cross.title: periapsis: A Comprehensive Orbital Fitting Package
cross.summary: We introduce a new Python package \texttt{periapsis}, which computes posterior distributions for a variety of orbital parameters given astrometric and/or radial velocity data. \texttt{periapsis} not only returns posterior distributions, but also a variety of statistics assessing convergence and fit metrics as well as plotting capabilities for visualizing the orbital systems. In this paper, we describe our various methods for fitting Keplerian orbits to both astrometric and radial velocity data. We then show the breadth of binary systems that \texttt{periapsis} can characterize by comparing our computed parameters with known orbital systems. Finally, we discuss how \texttt{periapsis} will be a helpful tool for future data releases like \textit{Gaia} DR4 and \textit{Roman}.

cross.title: A Bayesian Approach to Prioritizing the Follow-Up of Near-Earth Objects
cross.summary: We present pneo, a Bayesian classifier that computes the probability that a single-night tracklet belongs to a near-Earth object (NEO), using only its sky position, angular motion, and apparent magnitude. A tracklet does not determine the object's distance or radial velocity, so pneo integrates a model of the Solar System's small-body populations over all bound orbits consistent with it. The result is the exact posterior probability under that model, with no tuned scores or separately chosen priors: its classifications are optimal for the adopted model, and its probabilities are calibrated. On real discovery tracklets from the NEO Confirmation Page, the classifier is well calibrated and its selection is 1.14 times purer than that of digest2, the classifier now in use, at the same completeness. The advantage grows at Rubin's depth, where the faint background of main-belt and more distant objects is still largely undiscovered. On simulated tracklets to that depth, its selection is 2 times purer than that of digest2 (96% against 48%). On the Rubin alert stream and Rubin Data Preview 2 its selection is 1.4-1.7 times purer than that of digest2, and its predicted NEO counts are close to those observed. By raising the fraction of follow-up targets that are NEOs, pneo could potentially double the effective capacity of NEO follow-up in the Rubin era.

repl.title: Flare driven habitability: Expanding life's potential around low-mass stars
repl.summary: The traditional definition of the circumstellar habitable zone (HZ) focuses on liquid water, but neglects the crucial role of ultraviolet (UV) radiation in prebiotic chemistry. Low-mass stars typically emit insufficient UV radiation for photochemistry throughout the liquid water HZs during quiescent states. However, frequent flares can provide substantial UV fluxes, potentially fostering habitable conditions. We refine the concept of a UV habitable zone (UV-HZ) by incorporating a temperature-dependent model for RNA precursor synthesis. Furthermore, we explore a parameterized spectral energy distribution model and adopt an empirical flare frequency distribution for flares on different stars to quantify their UV contribution. Applying this framework to different flaring stars, we find the UV-HZ around low-mass stars can extend to inner regions, and overlap with the traditional HZ in wide ranges. Apply the analysis to 9 planets around Kepler flaring stars, three planets are located within both the refined UV-HZ and liquid water habitable zone (LW-HZ) without causing ozone depletion. Our findings highlight the significant role of flares in expanding the potential for life around low-mass stars, offering a revised perspective on exoplanet habitability criteria.

repl.title: A comprehensive study of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko in the 2021/2022 apparition. II. Colorimetry, polarimetry, modeling
repl.summary: This paper presents the second part of our multi-technique observational study of comet 67P during its 2021-2022 apparition. While the first paper focused on photometry and spectroscopy, here we investigate the dust color and linear polarization of the coma. Imaging in the g-sdss and r-sdss filters was obtained with the 6-m BTA SAO Telescope, and aperture polarimetry was performed with the 2.6-m Shajn Telescope (CrAO) and the 2-m RCC Telescope. Observations at phase angles of 47.9 deg (6 October 2021) and 10.5 deg (6 February 2022) show negative polarization of about 0.5-2.5% at 10.5 deg and positive polarization of about 11% at 47.9 deg. The dust color was red, reaching about 0.8 mag near the nucleus and in the tail, and decreasing to about 0.2 mag in the coma and jet within 20,000 km of the nucleus. Spatial maps reveal a gradual decrease in color index and a corresponding increase in polarization with distance from the nucleus. Numerical modeling using ballistic particle-cluster aggregates composed of equal fractions of silicates and organics indicates that the coma is dominated by particles larger than 10 micrometers, while local polarization enhancements are consistent with regions containing smaller (1-10 micrometer) grains. Combining our aperture measurements with published data from four previous apparitions confirms that comet 67P belongs to the high-polarization class. The unusually high positive polarization observed during the 2021/22 apparition, together with the relatively isotropic coma morphology, suggests that the dust properties may have changed after the 2015/16 apparition.

repl.title: Linking Outer Solar System Objects in Archival DECam Imaging: A Multi-year Linker Tested on Held-out Known Objects, and 273 Multi-opposition Candidates Including Six L4 Neptune Trojans, Two Retrograde Objects and Ten with a > 150 au
repl.summary: I link single-night detections in public DECam imaging: 74% of the NOIRLab Source Catalog DR2 (2012-2019) sky with four or more nights, and my extraction from 149,421 exposures (2020-2026). Of 931 secure known objects, single-season linking recovers 22.1-25.0%, a multi-year linker 26.5%, together 36.2%. The multi-year rule, fixed before its held-out tests, recovers 68% of DES objects brighter than r=23.5 in a strip of its footprint and 14 of 47 known objects outside it. Its shifted-sky controls, complete for 162 of 165 blocks, return no candidate. This limits pure chance alignments, not links that mix real and chance detections. An identity check by orbit with 3,110 joint fits finds no designated object among the candidates. Searches beyond 79 au recover, blind, only 2014 UZ224, Gonggong and Chiminigagua. The catalogue has 273 undesignated candidates with orbits from two or more oppositions, whose linked detections were re-measured on the images; of the 189 of version 2, 41 were then detected on two or more nights that their fits did not use. Listed apart are 92 weaker entries and 30 designated objects, 17 of them Rubin discoveries with 2.9-13.2 yr of arc before discovery. Six are candidate L4 Neptune Trojans whose orbits and clones librate for 10 Myr (one reported independently by Jongma 2026, mostly from other data), two are retrograde candidates and ten have a>150 au. There is no follow-up or validated selection function. The Minor Planet Center has astrometry of 38 objects; unreleased positions are available on request, in confidence.

repl.title: Thermal evolution of Uranus and Neptune, hydrogen-water phase separation and the role of methane
repl.summary: Adiabatic evolution models of Uranus and Neptune with constant compositional stratification miss their observed luminosities: Uranus is fainter than commonly predicted, while improved equations of state (EoS) have recently led to a brightness problem for Neptune. In adiabatic models of Jupiter and Saturn, helium rain is thought to enhance luminosity. In the ice giants, hydrogen-water phase separation (H2-H2O demixing) with water rain has recently been predicted. We aim to understand how H2-H2O demixing and the EoS of water influence the luminosity of Uranus and Neptune. We use state-of-the-art EoS of H, He, H2O, and the H2-H2O phase diagram to build adiabatic three-layer models of the present-day structure that match the observed gravity field and the phase diagram. We compute evolution tracks with and without demixing, and for Neptune, with and without latent heat and methane, for which we provide an updated large-scale EoS including entropy. Without demixing, adiabatic Neptune with the revised AQUA EoS, without methane or latent heat, cools to its observed luminosity within 4.5 Gyr, in good agreement with the age of the Solar system. Applying the same assumptions to Uranus would require a Bond albedo of 0.43 to explain its luminosity. With demixing, the radii expand while the luminosity decreases. For Uranus, demixing leads to an equilibrium evolution with the incident flux that naturally explains its faintness. Demixing also makes Neptune fainter. Methane reduces the radius expansion but not the faintness problem. Favored Neptune models include demixing and methane at an initial C/O ratio of $\sim$1 due to CO ice accretion, with cooling times of $\lesssim 4 Gyr. Neptune requires an additional heat source unless its structure is primordial and the outer envelope is ice-poor, while hydrogen-water phase separation is an option to explain the structure and faintness of Uranus.

repl.title: Hyrax: An Extensible Framework for Rapid ML Experimentation and Unsupervised Discovery in the Era of Rubin, Roman, and Euclid
repl.summary: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Roman Space Telescope, Euclid, and other next-generation surveys will deliver imaging, spectroscopic, and time-domain data at scales that increasingly shift the bottleneck in astronomical machine learning (ML) projects from model design to infrastructure. We present Hyrax, an open-source, modular, GPU-enabled Python framework that supports the full ML lifecycle in astronomy: from data acquisition and training to inference and experiment comparison, with capabilities including multimodal dataset support, integrated vector databases for similarity search, and interactive two- and three-dimensional latent-space exploration for unsupervised discovery. We demonstrate Hyrax's versatility through five representative applications on real survey data: (i) unsupervised representation learning on $\sim 4\times10^5$ Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Data Preview 1 (DP1) galaxies, surfacing new merger and low-surface-brightness candidates missing from reference Euclid and Dark Energy Survey catalogs, while also isolating imaging artifacts -- all without labeled training data; (ii) hybrid density-based clustering for identifying cluster-scale gravitational lens candidates in DP1 data; (iii) multimodal early-time transient classification in the Zwicky Transient Facility leveraging light curves, spectra, images, and metadata; (iv) supervised false-positive filtering in shift-and-stack searches for distant solar system objects in the Dark Energy Camera Ecliptic Exploration Project survey; and (v) supervised detection of semi-resolved dwarf galaxies in Hyper Suprime-Cam and LSST-like imaging using synthetic source injection. Together, these results demonstrate that Hyrax provides astronomy-specific ML infrastructure that enables systematic discovery and rapid methodological iteration across next-generation astronomical surveys.

Hyrax provides robust, astronomy-specific implementations for all of these components—allowing researchers to focus on developing their own models—while also offering a selection of pre-built models for common use cases. This depiction is inspired by the analogous diagram in Sculley et al. [88] .

Schematic of the primary modules within Hyrax. (1) The workflow begins with hyrax.download() for parallelized data retrieval from supported surveys or custom user-provided sources. (2) Retrieved data are organized into flexible, astronomy-tailored ML datasets. (3) The training module ( hyrax.train() ) offers intelligent pre-caching, live monitoring, logging, and multi-GPU support, via e.g., PyTorch, MLflow, Optuna [ 5 ] , and TensorBoard, (4) Both supervised and unsupervised models are supported, with inference for either performed via hyrax.infer() . (5) For unsupervised workflows, outputs can be stored in flexible vector databases (e.g., LanceDB 7 7 7 https://github.com/lancedb/lancedb , ChromaDB 8 8 8 https://github.com/chroma-core/chroma ) to enable rapid similarity search and clustering. (6) Built-in visualization modules provide interactive 2D/3D latent-space exploration (via e.g., three.js 9 9 9 https://threejs.org/ , HoloViews 10 10 10 https://holoviews.org/ , Datashader 11 11 11 https://datashader.org/ ), linking model outputs back to source data and facilitating rapid discovery in large survey datasets.

Training ML models on survey-scale imaging data requires efficient access to potentially millions of image cutouts. This block diagram shows how Hyrax’s LSSTDataset class addresses this: survey patches are retrieved via the Rubin Butler and cached at the patch level on local storage, preventing repeated queries for the same sky region. During training, image cutouts are preemptively generated on the fly from the cached patches via multi-threaded requests and streamed directly to the ML model on the GPU, enabling efficient training in both on-platform (e.g., Rubin Science Platform) and offline environments (e.g., HPC cluster with access to the Rubin Butler).

Diagram of the primary components that control the flow of data during training and inference in Hyrax. Data are read by an appropriate DatasetClass that exposes components of the data to DataProvider . The DataProvider prepares a combined dataset based on the user data request configuration. The ML engine will request data samples for training or inference, which are then furnished by DataProvider . The DataProvider can also be configured to preload items from disk and cache them in memory to speed up the training process. In practice, we found that this often sped up training epochs by an order of magnitude.

Model comparison and experiment tracking in Hyrax via its native MLflow integration. The static version of this figure shows the MLflow interface populated automatically during Hyrax training runs, displaying loss curves, evaluation metrics, and hyperparameters for multiple experiments executed under a common configuration framework. This enables systematic and easy comparison of models across different datasets and hyperparameter choices without additional user bookkeeping. The animated version of this figure (available in the online version and at this link ) demonstrates interactive exploration of this interface, including filtering and sorting runs, inspecting metric histories, and drilling down into individual model configurations during and after training.

The left column shows query images, while the right columns show nearest neighbors retrieved via the search_by_vector() method. In the top row, a query galaxy exhibiting extended low–surface-brightness features retrieves neighbors with similarly diffuse outer light. In the bottom row, a merger/close-pair system is used as the query, and the retrieved neighbors display comparable interacting/multi-component morphologies.
